Mr. Owsley is a 60-year-old man who has presented with a number of cognitive impairments and has been diagnosed with a non-
degenerative dementia. Which of the following is an example of a non- degenerative dementia?
questions.explanation:
Alcoholic dementia is a non-degenerative process as the damage caused ceases once alcohol is no longer being consumed. The other
disorders listed are degenerative and progressive. Other examples of non-degenerative dementia include: cancer with or without brain
metastases; normal-pressure hydrocephalus; subdural haematoma; hypothyroidism; vitamin B12 de�ciency; and neurosyphilis.

questions.question_text:
Mrs Terry is a 78-year-old woman who has recently been diagnosed with mild Alzheimer's dementia. She is aware of the diagnosis and is
keen to start treatment. She has recently been started on Donepezil after the bene�ts and risks were explained to her. Which of the
following physiological parameters is the most important to monitor in her case?
questions.explanation:
Donepezil can be associated with bradycardia, heart block and syncope. Heart rate must be monitored when this medication is started and
when the dose is increased.

questions.question_text:
Mrs Brown is a 72-year-old lady who has recently been diagnosed with lung cancer whilst on the medical ward. The geriatrician looking after
her is seeing if it is possible to rationalise her medication from her notes. She has been on a long-term prescription of diazepam 5mg BD
from her GP. The indication for this is not clear. Which of the following diagnoses are associated with prescription benzodiazepine use in
older people?
questions.explanation:
According to the below study female sex, mild cognitive impairment, depression, panic disorder and suicidal ideation were associated with
benzodiazepine dependence in community dwelling older people. (Ref: Voyer P, Preville M, Roussel ME, Berbiche D, Beland SG. Factors
associated with benzodiazepine dependence among community-dwelling seniors, J Community Health Nurs , 2009, vol. 26 (pg. 101-13))

questions.question_text:
The Driving Vehicle Licensing Agency (UK) requests that they are informed if people are diagnosed with certain mental illnesses as these
may impact on their ability to drive. Which of the following diagnoses is most commonly associated with dangerous driving?
questions.explanation:
Dementia, except potentially in the very early stages, is associated with signi�cant risks around driving and the DVLA generally advises that
people stop driving after they receive a diagnosis. The other disorders listed can be associated with dangerous driving but this is dependent
upon the symptoms an individual experience, whether they are experiencing an episode of illness.

questions.question_text:
Mrs Larkin attends the diagnostic memory clinic with her husband. She is 55 years old and currently working as a teacher but has noticed
that she is �nding it increasingly di�cult to plan lessons and has lost her con�dence in social situations. Her husband has noticed she is
repetitive and is worried because she got lost driving to their holiday house despite usually knowing the route well. What is the most
common neurodegenerative disorder in those aged less than 65 years?
questions.explanation:
The most common cause of young onset dementia (ie: in those aged 30 - 64) is Alzheimer's disease, followed by vascular, followed by
frontotemporal, alcohol related, dementia with Lewy bodies, and Huntington's disease. (Ref: Sampson EL, Warren JD, Rossor MN. Young
onset dementia. Postgraduate Medical Journal 2004;80:125-139).

questions.question_text:
Mrs Jones is a retired science teacher and her husband has recently been diagnosed with dementia. She is interested to know how his
dementia is classi�ed. Which of the following dementia is correctly matched with the brain area it a�ects in the initial stages of the disease
process?
questions.explanation:
Alzheimer's disease and frontotemporal dementia are both cortical. Vascular dementia, Progressive Supranuclear Palsy, Huntington's
disease, multiple sclerosis, Parkinson's disease and hydrocephalus are sub-cortical. Dementia with Lewy bodies is considered to be cortico-
subcortical (Mixed type) (Ref: Shaik, S. S. and Varma, A. R. (2012), Di�erentiating the dementias: a neurological approach. Prog. Neurol.
Psychiatry, 16: 11-18. doi:10.1002/pnp.224

questions.question_text:
Mrs Tanya Walters is a 75-year-old woman with an existing diagnosis of mild Alzheimer's dementia. Over the past 5 weeks her family have
noticed that she has been persistent low in mood, withdrawn and has shown no interest in activities, which she used to enjoy. On
assessment, she expresses feeling “useless” and constantly tired. Which of the following would be the most appropriate management plan
at this point?

options.text: Urine dip and blood tests to exclude organic causes

correct_answer.text: Urine dip and blood tests to exclude organic causes

questions.explanation:
While patients with dementia can become depressed and require antidepressant medication or other interventions, they are more
vulnerable than the general population to developing mood disturbance in response to organic illness, which may not be immediately
apparent. It is prudent to check for organic illness before o�ering an antidepressant. Remember that MDD is a disorder of exclusion in the
elderly. SSRIs are more appropriate than tricyclics in the older population who may have cardiac disease or be on other medications with
potential drug interactions.

questions.question_text:
Mr Benjamin Wyles is a 77-year-old man with a history of recurrent depressive disorder. He is currently experiencing a severe episode of
depression and his appetite is very poor. His illness has not responded to 3 adequate trials of antidepressants. Which of the following is the
most appropriate treatment for him at this stage?
questions.explanation:
The patient is experiencing a severe treatment resistant episode of depression with marked appetite disturbance. It would be reasonable to
treat him with ECT to achieve rapid improvement and address his appetite disturbance while also continuing antidepressants. Older patients
can receive ECT and often respond well.

questions.question_text:
Older people who express suicidal ideation or attempt suicide are at greater future risk than younger patients. Which of the following is
most associated with suicide in old age?
questions.explanation:
Avoidant and anankastic personality disorder are associated with increased risk of suicide in older people. Histrionic personality disorder is
associated with a lower risk of suicide. All personality disorders are associated with an increased risk of suicidal ideation. Male gender, being
widowed and having a lower openness to experience are associated with an increased risk of suicide in older age.

questions.question_text:
Mrs Lisbeth Slander is a 79-year-old woman who has progressively developed loss of memory, visual hallucinations and intermittent
irritability over the course of several months. Which of the following would be the most appropriate treatment for her condition?
questions.explanation:
This is most likely to represent Lewy Body Dementia, which is characterized by memory impairment, perceptual disturbances and mood
changes. The �rst line of treatment is acetyl cholinesterase inhibitors, such as Rivastigamine.

questions.question_text:
Mr Aubrey is a 36-year-old man with a diagnosis of panic disorder. He is unwilling to have talking therapy but is asking about medication
options. Which of the following would be most appropriate medication to consider initially for treating panic disorder?
questions.explanation: SSRIs like Sertraline are recommended as the �rst line medication for panic disorder. Other antidepressants could potentially be used.

questions.question_text:
Terry is a 43-year-old man with bipolar disorder and is on Lithium treatment. He is now presenting with mixed a�ective state. His recent
Lithium level is 0.8. What would be your next step?
questions.explanation:
Mixed a�ective state should be treated as manic episode. The best strategy in this situation is to start him on an antipsychotic medication. Li
levels are optimal and to increase further could risk toxicity.

questions.question_text:
Mr. Jameson is a 35-year-old man who has recently been diagnosed with ADHD of moderate severity. He is keen to receive treatment due to
the impact his symptoms have at his work. Which of the following are recommended as the �rst line treatment in adult ADHD?
questions.explanation:
Medication is the mainstay of treatment for adults with ADHD. Methylphenidate is the �rst line treatment, with atomoxetine and
dexamphetamine being options if this is ine�ective. CBT can be trialled if medication does not show positive e�ects.

questions.question_text:
Mrs. Kelvin is a 42-year-old woman with a diagnosis of schizophrenia. She has struggled to take her oral medication in the past and has now
agreed to have a depot instead. Which of the following depot mediations requires at least 2 hours monitoring after it has been given?
questions.explanation:
Patients receiving olanzapine as a depot must be monitored for at least 2 hours after administration. Olanzapine post-injection syndrome
has been estimated to occur after 0.07% of olanzapine depot injections and in approximately 1.4% of treated patients. Post-injection
syndrome includes a range of signs and symptoms such as sedation and delirium that are consistent with olanzapine overdose. Other
symptoms include dizziness, weakness, aggression, ataxia, hypertension and seizures. Extrapyramidal symptoms are also reported, such as
tremor, dystonia, akathisia, and tardive dyskinesia. It generally starts around 1 hour after administration and resolves after 24-72 hours.

questions.question_text:
John is a 29-year-old man with a long history of paranoid schizophrenia and recently started on a new antipsychotic medication. His baseline
BP was 130/70. During his weekly review, his blood pressure was 160/90. Which of the following antipsychotic drug is most associated with
hypertension?
questions.explanation:
Most case reports implicate clozapine with some clearly describing normal blood pressure before clozapine was introduced, a sharp rise
during treatment and return to normal when clozapine was discontinued. Data available through the committee on safety of medicines
yellow card system in the UK indicate that clozapine is the antipsychotic drug most associated with hypertension. There are a small number
of reports on Olanzapine, Risperidone, Quetiapine and aripiprazole. (Ref: The Maudsley prescribing guidelines- 11th edition; pg no-122)

questions.question_text:
Miss Lodge is a 29-year-old woman who has been referred to an outpatient clinic and brought by her family. She receives an MMSE but
performs poorly. She was irritable. She states that she has no time to complete the test and that she needs to speak to the Chief Constable.
Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
The most likely diagnosis is an episode of mania in view of the grandiose delusion she describes and irritability with the assessment process.
The other diagnoses would be unlikely in a person of this age, unless there was some evidence to support them.

questions.question_text:
Miss Newton is a 36-year-old woman with a diagnosis of treatment resistant schizophrenia. She is receiving an optimum medication regime
for her and is currently an inpatient in a rehabilitation unit with a view towards reintegrating her into "normal life“. Which of the following
will be most likely to help her return to independent living?
questions.explanation:
There is signi�cant evidence to indicate that supported employment, particularly Individual Placement and Support, is e�ective in enabling
people with chronic psychosis to function more e�ectively in the community.

questions.question_text:
Mr. Vano is a 24-year-old man who has recently been admitted to a general hospital. Which of the following physical health conditions
would be most likely to increase his risk of suicide?
questions.explanation: A history of a traumatic brain injury may increase the subsequent risk of suicide 9-fold. HIV positive status can double the risk of suicide.

questions.question_text:
Mr Mullen is a 30-year-old soldier who returned from Afghanistan 3 months ago. Towards the end of his tour of duty he witnessed an
unexpected attack where his close friend and fellow soldier was shot and killed. He managed to escape but was shot in his left leg in the
cross �re and continues to experience pain. He visits his GP as he is concerned about persistent �ashbacks of the event and a sense of
being on edge all the time. This has been occurring for the last 1 month. Which features would not be consistent with a diagnosis of PTSD?

options.text: Symptoms occurring within 6 months of the original trauma

questions.explanation:
Recurring dreams, di�culty concentrating and irritability are common features of PTSD. Symptoms typically occur within 6 months (though
in delayed onset can occur more than 6 months after the trauma). Hypersomnia is not a common feature in PTSD as the presentation is
generally one of hyperarousal.

questions.question_text:
Miss Saunders is a 25-year-old woman with bipolar disorder, who has been referred to your outpatient clinic by her GP with a likely episode
of depression of moderate severity. Which of the following symptoms is she most likely to exhibit?
questions.explanation:
Depression and somatoform disorder are highly co-morbid, with around 50% of patients with depression or anxiety having signi�cant
somatoform symptoms. Nihilistic delusions or auditory hallucinations would indicate a diagnosis of psychotic depression, which would
therefore be severe. Over talkativeness and agitation are more likely in mania or a mixed a�ective episode.

questions.question_text:
Mr Mathey is a 26-year-old man who has been brought into A&E with fever, confusion, agitation and auditory hallucinations over the last
several hours. He has a lumbar puncture as part of his assessment, which demonstrates lymphocytosis, normal glucose and increased
protein. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Herpes encephalitis is the most likely diagnosis in view of the acute onset of symptoms suggesting systemic in�ammation and neurological
involvement. Patients commonly have marked lymphocytosis, increased red cells, increased protein and low or normal glucose levels in CSF.

questions.question_text:
Mr Davidson is a 37-year-old man who has a diagnosis of bipolar a�ective disorder and has been admitted to a mental health unit with a
mixed a�ective episode. He had discontinued his previous medication. Which of the following treatments would be most appropriate for
managing his current episode?
questions.explanation:
Valproate has established e�ectiveness in mixed a�ective episodes, as do atypical antipsychotics. Mixed a�ective episodes do not appear to
respond well to Lithium, in contrast to its e�ectiveness in classical mania. There is no evidence for Lamotrigine in mania or mixed a�ective
episodes.

questions.question_text:
Mr Harris is a 42-year-old man with a diagnosis of treatment resistant schizophrenia who is currently stable. He is a heavy smoker and
requires a Clozapine dose of 1000mg daily to maintain his serum clozapine level in a therapeutic range. He has been admitted to a general
hospital following a generalised seizure in the community. The medical team does not identify any intracranial or systemic cause for his
seizure. Which of the following should be done to reduce the risk of further seizure activity?
questions.explanation:
In this case, adding sodium valproate would likely be the most appropriate option. It has a broad spectrum of anti-seizure activity and does
not have a major impact upon clozapine metabolism. Reducing clozapine dose is an option in some patients but not for this patient as it
would likely lead to his serum clozapine level being below the therapeutic range. Carbamazepine induces the enzymes that metabolise
clozapine, reducing the serum clozapine level. Adding amisulpride would likely increase the risk of seizure activity, as it will lower the seizure
threshold. And if the patient is treatment resistant, they likely require clozapine; changing to an alternative antipsychotic could lead to an
increase in psychotic symptoms.

questions.question_text:
Mrs. Ginner is a 34-year-old woman with a diagnosis of anorexia nervosa. She has been admitted to a general hospital due to concerns
about dehydration and profound weight loss. Disturbance of which of the following electrolytes most requires monitoring during the
refeeding of profoundly unweight patients?
questions.explanation:
While disturbance of all electrolytes can occur in profoundly underweight patients, it is serum phosphate levels that are most important to
monitor. Refeeding increases the release of insulin, which requires phosphate, magnesium and potassium. These are usually depleted body-
wide. Serum phosphate is also depleted by the formation of phosphate-containing carbohydrate compounds in the muscle and liver. If
refeeding is done gradually, these electrolyte disturbances can gradually be corrected. If done too rapidly, the body does not have the time
or capacity to respond to the changes in serum electrolytes, leading to profound hypophosphataemia. Cardiac arrhythmias are the most
common cause of death from refeeding syndrome, with other signi�cant risks including confusion, coma and convulsions and cardiac
failure.

questions.question_text:
Mr Maloney is a 27-year-old man admitted to the surgical ward following emergency appendectomy. On the �rst postoperative night, he is
seen to be restless and wanting to know if he can leave the ward. When his history is reviewed it is noted he is a heroin user, and usually
smokes daily. Which of the following is not an early sign of opiate withdrawal?
questions.explanation:
The early signs of opiate withdrawal include agitation, anxiety, muscle aches, increased tearing, insomnia, runny nose, sweating, yawning.
Later symptoms of withdrawal include abdominal cramping, diarrhoea, dilated pupils, goose bumps, nausea, vomiting.

questions.question_text:
Schizophrenia is associated with a variety of clinical symptoms, aside from hallucinations and delusions. This includes cognitive de�cits.
Which of the following is most likely to be impaired when people with schizophrenia receive cognitive testing?
questions.explanation:
Working memory is most likely to be impaired in schizophrenia. This can have e�ects upon other cognitive functions, such as selective
attention and abstract reasoning.

questions.question_text:
Mrs. Manner is 60-year-old woman who has presented to her GP in a distressed state and reports that she has been experiencing a burning
sensation in all her limbs. She is examined and has investigations but no physical cause is found. Which of the following is the most likely
diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
This is most likely to be somatoform pain disorder, which is characterised by chronic pain that does not �t with any recognised clinical
syndromes or neurological pathways and is often associated with marked psychological distress. Somatisation disorder most commonly
presents with symptoms related to somatic organ systems, such as gastrointestinal, respiratory and cardiac.

questions.question_text:
Mr Lewis is a 24-year-old man with a diagnosis of social phobia. He has been referred to your outpatient clinic for advice on medication, as
he does not feel able to engage in psychological interventions at this time. Which of the following medications would be most likely to be
bene�cial for him?
questions.explanation:
SSRIs are most commonly used in social phobia and have the best evidence base. Pregabalin is used for generalised anxiety disorder but
does not have a su�cient evidence base for social phobia. Clomipramine could be used for social phobia, but is not preferred; its main use
is in OCD if an SSRI is ine�ective. Beta-blockers can be used for performance anxiety and can reduce physical symptoms of anxiety in a given
situation but are not recommended for social phobia. Benzodiazepines can be used to manage severe anxiety but do not manage the
underlying beliefs and are dependence-forming; they are not generally recommended.

questions.question_text:
Miss Megan is a 39-year-old woman who has a history of presenting to various doctors, including GPs, out-of-hours services and private
clinics. She is insistent that she has multiple sclerosis and that she is investigated for this despite there being no evidence of this during
history taking or examination. When she is reassured that there is no reason for investigations and there is no evidence of MS she tends to
become angry before leaving the clinic. Which of the following is most likely to be the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
This is most likely to represent hypochondriasis. In this disorder an individual has an overvalued idea that they are ill, often with a speci�c
disorder, and repeatedly presents to health services to con�rm this. They can be temporarily reassured in some cases, but can be irritable if
healthcare sta�s do not accede to their requests.

questions.question_text:
Mr Powell is a 55-year-old man. He has been picked up by the police and taken to local Emergency Department as being found a substantial
distance from his home with no memory of going there. There is no physical cause found for this and his concentration and cognition are
intact on testing in the hospital. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
This appears to represent a dissociative fugue whereby an individual, usually after encountering a stressor, will wander in the community
until they are found or they come out of the fugue. They will have no memory of their travels although they may have appeared normal to
those they encountered. Their cognition is usually normal once the episode has passed.

questions.question_text:
Lithium is a highly e�ective medication for bipolar disorder, which must be maintained within a speci�c therapeutic range to prevent
subtherapeutic levels or toxicity. Which of the following medications is most associated with neurotoxicity when prescribed with lithium?
questions.explanation:
Haloperidol, �uphenazine and �upenthixol have been associated with irreversible toxic encephalopathy when combined with lithium, and
are particularly associated with neurotoxicity, even when lithium is within the therapeutic range.

questions.question_text:
Mrs. Galsworthy is a 32-year-old woman with a diagnosis of OCD. She is currently under your care in an outpatient clinic and is due to start
active treatment. She and her husband have asked about her likely prognosis. Which of the following is most associated with a positive
prognosis in the short term in OCD?
questions.explanation: An early and positive response to SSRI treatment is predictive of remission of OCD symptoms.

questions.question_text:
Mrs. Vaughn is a 38-year-old woman with a diagnosis of epilepsy. She has recently presented to her GP with symptoms of low mood,
inability to enjoy her usual activities and poor sleep. Which of the following is most likely to increase the risk of developing depression
among people with epilepsy?
questions.explanation:
Complex partial seizures and absence of secondary generalized tonic–clonic seizures are risk factors for depression. Treatment with
clonazepam, frequent hospitalizations (drug resistance) and lack of occupational activity are additional signi�cant contributing factors.

questions.question_text:
Mr Howard Hughes is a 43-year-old man who has repeatedly attended his GP surgery and local A&E with concerns that something is
blocking his throat. He has had numerous negative investigations, including direct visualisation of his pharynx, which can temporarily
reassure him. Nevertheless, he continues to present himself. When asked, he describes a sense of something in his throat and is clearly very
anxious. This is most likely to be
questions.explanation:
This is most likely to be hypochondriasis as the patient has an overvalued idea about a particular diagnosis. In somatisation disorder,
patients describe numerous and often changeable physical symptoms. Patients experiencing psychotic symptoms would generally not be
reassured, even temporarily, by negative investigation �ndings. Note that DSM-5 prefers the term Somatic Symptom Disorder for the same
presentation.

questions.question_text:
Post-natal depression can lead to signi�cant distress in new mothers and impair their ability to bond with and care for their newborn
children. What percentage of new mothers su�ers from postnatal depression?
questions.explanation:
It is thought that 10-15% of new mothers experience post-natal depression, with rates reducing to <10% after 12 weeks postpartum. Ref:
Leahy-Warren et al., Arch Psychiatr Nurs. 2011 Jun;25(3):174-84

questions.question_text:
Inpatient suicide rates in the UK have reduced signi�cantly since 2000. Which of the following is thought to have contributing most to this
decrease?

options.text: Use of formal risk assessment tools

questions.explanation:
In the UK, hanging was the reported method in 77% of inpatient suicides between 1999 and 2007. The most common ligature points were
doors, hooks or handles, windows, belts, and sheets or towels. Removal of ligature points had a signi�cant impact on the rate of inpatient
suicides, though the use of shoelaces, doors, and windows increased over time. Ref; Bowers, L.; Dack, C.; Gul, N.; Thomas, B.; James, K.
(2011) Learning from prevented suicide in psychiatric inpatient care: An analysis of data from the National Patient Safety Agency.
International Journal of Nursing Studies 48 (12) 1459-1465

questions.question_text:
People with schizophrenia can have certain cognitive impairments that are present when they are not experiencing an episode of psychosis.
Which of the following is most common?
questions.explanation: The most common cognitive impairments in schizophrenia are those around executive functioning and working memory.

questions.question_text:
Mr Charlie Simms is a 26-year-old man who has recently been diagnosed with schizophrenia. Once he has recovered he is keen to know
more about his prognosis and what factors might have an impact on it. Which of the following factors is most likely to support a favourable
prognosis?
questions.explanation:
A family history of a�ective disorder is associated with a positive prognosis, as is having a�ective symptoms during episodes of illness. Acute
onset, short duration of untreated symptoms, older age of onset, good premorbid functioning, being in a stable relationship and having a
good support system are all positive prognostic factors in schizophrenia.

questions.question_text:
Puerperal psychosis is a psychotic illness that tends to occur shortly after a woman gives birth. Which of the following is the most common
presentation?
questions.explanation:
Prominent a�ective symptoms and unusual behaviour are the most common presenting symptoms in puerperal psychosis. This is often
associated with profound anxiety and this can be associated with persecutory ideation. Many patients later satisfy the criteria for psychotic
bipolar disorder.

questions.question_text:
Mr Edward Hughes is a 23-year-old man with autism spectrum disorder and moderate intellectual impairment. He lives in a placement and
has been demonstrating aggressive behaviour over the last several months. Attempts to identify the cause of his distress or address his
behaviour via non-pharmacological methods have been fruitless. Which of the following would be the most appropriate treatment for him?
questions.explanation:
Risperidone and Aripiprazole have the greatest evidence base for the pharmacological management of aggression in ASD. Other second-
and �rst-generation antipsychotics, antiepileptic medications, lithium, naltrexone and N-acetylcysteine have also been used although with
less evidence being available for these agents.

questions.question_text:
Mr Neil Peterson is a 36-year-old man who is currently experiencing a moderate depressive episode. He is struggling to motivate himself to
engage with his usual activities and is due to be assessed for behavioural activation therapy. Which of the following will this include?
questions.explanation:
Assessment for behavioural activation therapy includes identi�cation of TRAP (Trigger, Response, Avoidance Pattern) with the avoidance
including direct avoidance, rumination and use of alcohol, drugs and other maladaptive coping strategies. The aim is to replace this with
TRAC (Trigger, Response, Alternate Coping response). Ref: Weinstock LM, Munroe MK, Miller IW. Behavioral activation for the treatment of
atypical depression: a pilot open trial. Behavior modi�cation. 2011 Jul;35(4):403-24.

questions.question_text:
Mrs Susan Matthews is a 42-year-old woman with a previous diagnosis of bipolar a�ective disorder. She has been well without medication
for three years but has now presented with a clear-cut episode of depression. Which of the following would be most appropriate to treat
her?
questions.explanation:
NICE recommends that individuals with a diagnosis of bipolar depression, who are not currently receiving medication, should be prescribed
either Olanzapine and Fluoxetine in combo or Quetiapine by itself as �rst line treatment. Patients can choose to have Olanzapine without
Fluoxetine if desired (but not the antidepressant alone). Lamotrigine can also be o�ered if the above therapies are ine�ective or the patient
expresses a preference for it. Ref:

questions.question_text:
ECT is a highly e�ective intervention in those with severe episodes of depression, which are treatment resistant or associated with risk to
life. Which of the following is true about ECT?

options.text: An ECT-induced seizure lasting longer than 2 minutes should be pharmacologically aborted
A history of Ischemic heart disease is an absolute contraindication for ECT
ECT can only be delivered for inpatients
Seizures on EEG last longer than the physical seizure
Antidepressants should be discontinued while ECT is delivered.

correct_answer.text: Seizures on EEG last longer than the physical seizure

questions.explanation:
It is common for seizure activity on the EEG to continue for longer than the physical movements, particularly as patients receiving ECT will
have also have been administered a muscle relaxant. Ref: Fink M, Abrams R. EEG monitoring in ECT: a guide to treatment e�cacy. Psychiatric
Times, May. 1998 May 1;15(5).

questions.question_text:
Tina Keyes is a 2-year-old girl who was born with a cleft palate, which is in the process of being surgically repaired. She demonstrated
evidence of development delay during her �rst year and it is now thought that she will likely have a degree of intellectual disability. Which of
the following medications taken during pregnancy is most likely to have contributed to these problems?
questions.explanation:
Sodium valproate should not be prescribed to women of childbearing age unless other therapies are ine�ective or inappropriate. If taken
throughout pregnancy, about 10% of infants will have a congenital malformation and 40% will have a degree of developmental delay and
intellectual impairment. Sertraline and other SSRIs are associated with a small increase in the risk of congenital malformations. Lithium was
associated with an increase in the risk of congenital malformations, particularly Ebstein's anomaly. Benzodiazepines were considered to be
associated with cleft lip and palate, but recent studies indicate that the risk is much lower than what was thought before. Antipsychotics,
with the exception of risperidone, which shows a small increase in the risk of cardiac defects, are not associated with congenital
abnormalities or developmental problems.

questions.question_text:
Mr Vincent Payes is a 38-year-old man with a diagnosis of paranoid schizophrenia. He has had a recent relapse, which has been successfully
treated with Olanzapine, but he reports that it makes him rather sedated during the day, including when he is driving. It appears likely that it
is impairing his ability to drive. Which of the following should be done?

options.text: Advise the patient to stop driving and report to the DVLA themselves
Advise the patient to continue to drive but be cautious
Advise the patient to omit the Olanzapine if they have to drive the next day
Report the patient's inability to drive to the DVLA directly

correct_answer.text: Advise the patient to stop driving and report to the DVLA themselves

questions.explanation:
The patient needs to stop driving if their medication may be impairing their ability to do so safely. It is usually appropriate to advise the
patient to stop driving and inform the DVLA. It may then be appropriate to modify their prescription so they are not so sedated during the
day, provided this does not compromise their mental wellbeing. If a patient will not inform the DVLA himself or herself, then it is appropriate
to contact them directly. The patient's con�dentiality can be breached for this purpose.

questions.question_text:
Abdominal pain is a common presenting symptom amongst children seen in paediatric practice. Which of the following is true regarding
abdominal pain in children?

options.text: Abdominal pain related to anxiety in children is usually very well localised to one spot
Abdominal pain is usually associated with clear bowel symptoms
Abdominal pain in children usually responds readily to medical interventions
Abdominal pain is usually associated with a persistent disturbance in appetite
Abdominal pain is a common symptom of anxiety in children

correct_answer.text: Abdominal pain is a common symptom of anxiety in children

questions.explanation:
Abdominal pain in children, whilst it can occasionally be due to signi�cant organic pathology, is usually ill de�ned and without clearly
associated physical symptoms. It is commonly associated with anxiety and worry. Ref; Cunningham NR, et al. Importance of addressing
anxiety in youth with functional abdominal pain: suggested guidelines for physicians. Journal of pediatric gastroenterology and nutrition.
2013 May;56(5):469.

questions.question_text:
Reading di�culties are relatively common and a�ected children and adults may need certain adaptations to engage with education and

questions.question_text: What is a systematic error?

An error leading to acceptance of null hypothesis

the experiment. They are not random errors. Bias is one type of systematic error that leads to an incorrect estimate of association, thus
resulting in either a false positive or false negative inference.

questions.question_text: A 40-year-old man is a long term cocaine user. He is likely to have abnormalities in which of the following cognitive domains?
